denJazykuText: Why today? 26 September is the European Day of Languages. The Council of Europe declared it in 2001 to celebrate Europe's some 225 indigenous languages and to encourage people to learn more of them. So today, instead of one Language of the Day, here are all {n} European languages in the atlas at once. Try greeting someone in a language that is new to you!

oDatech.nadpis: About the data and how the atlas was made
oDatech.uvod: The atlas is built on open databases put together by linguists from all over the world. Here is where everything comes from, what is certain and what is only an estimate.

p: Each dot is one language. The list of languages comes from Glottolog, an open database of the world's languages run by the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. The atlas takes everything Glottolog lists as a language and gives a location: {g} languages.
A dot stands where Glottolog places the language, usually in the middle of the area where it is spoken. Even a language spoken all over the world has just one dot, at its home.

Left out are only Glottolog's special bins: bookkeeping entries, languages known only by name and languages we know so little about that they cannot be classified. Esperanto, Interlingua and Interslavic have no dot because they did not arise in any one place; they are still in the list and in search.

There is no sharp line between a language and a dialect, and history and politics often play a part. The atlas follows Glottolog's decisions. That is why Bavarian has a dot but Australian English does not – Glottolog counts it as a variety of English. Dialects are listed on the language card, and searching for one finds its language.

Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin are very easy to understand for each other's speakers and rest on the same dialect base, Shtokavian. Linguistically they are close standard varieties of one shared language; officially and socially they are separate languages today. Glottolog lists them as one language, Serbo-Croatian, which has a dot on the globe. The atlas also has Serbian and Croatian as separate languages with a greeting, but they have no dot of their own. Hmong, on the other hand, is several languages in Glottolog and one entry in the atlas. That is why the list has {n} entries and the globe {g} dots.

{a} languages have a greeting, a pronunciation guide, a fun fact, a number of speakers and the area where they are spoken. All of this is written by hand. The fun facts are for children, but they have to be true and they are checked.
The pronunciation guide is only an approximation. Speaker numbers are rounded estimates and include people who learned the language.
The orange area on the globe is drawn by hand and approximate, not measured. There is no open data with exact language borders for the whole world.
The Listen button uses the voice your computer or phone has. For some languages it has none.
The painted postcards show the typical landscape and buildings of the region the language comes from. They are not pictures of particular places.
Vitality: the UNESCO scale (safe to extinct) based on Glottolog data.

Typology (word order, cases, tone, consonant inventory… – 24 features): WALS Online, the World Atlas of Language Structures (Dryer & Haspelmath 2013). WALS describes a sample of about 2,600 languages; the others have no value. For the map some values are merged into groups; the language card always shows the exact WALS value.
Number of sounds: PHOIBLE. Sample text: Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR in Unicode).
Speaker numbers: Wikidata; where missing, an estimate from Unicode CLDR.
Relatives and the family tree: the Glottolog tree, with Glottolog's branch names.
Nothing is made up: if a source has no data, the card does not show it.
Country borders and land come from Natural Earth (simplified, scale 1:110 million). Relief and the sea floor come from Natural Earth and NOAA ETOPO1.

navod.napoveda: Full guide – everything the atlas can do
navod.uvod: The atlas shows every language in the world on a spinning globe. Here is everything you can find in it and how to use it – with a mouse, a finger or the keyboard.

p: Spin: grab the globe with the mouse or one finger and drag. Zoom: the mouse wheel, two fingers apart, the + and − buttons in the bar at the bottom, or the + and − keys.
Each dot is one language. Click it to open its card. From 2× zoom, language names appear next to the dots (you can turn them off in View).
Click a country away from the dots and the atlas shows how many languages are spoken there and lights them up.
The Whole world button brings the globe back to the start. Clicking the logo in the top left does the same.

Languages with a greeting have a painted postcard of their region, the greeting, how to say it and a Listen button (it uses your device's voice). Below are labels – how many people speak it, its family and how endangered it is – and tabs with a fun fact, vitality and relatives.
Other languages have the tabs Overview (where it is spoken, how endangered it is, dialects), How it works (word order, cases, tones, sounds) and Relatives.
Light arcs on the globe lead from the selected language to its closest relatives. The family tree line shows the path from their common ancestor.
The chain button copies a link to the language that you can send to a friend. On a phone the card sits at the bottom: drag it up to enlarge it, down to shrink or close it.
You can search for a language, a country or a dialect. The cross in the search box clears it.
Sort languages by family, alphabetically or by continent. Big tiles with a greeting come first, the other languages below.

The Language of the Day changes every midnight and always says why it was chosen – it has its own day, or we are travelling around the world with it. All such days are in the Calendar of language days. On the European Day of Languages, 26 September, a card with all the European languages takes its place.
Surprise me picks a random language.
Family tree shows the tree of a whole language family. Drag to move it, use the wheel or two fingers to zoom, click a branch to focus on it and click a language to select it.
Vitality colours the languages by how endangered they are and shows a key. Tap the key to choose which levels to show.
View: auto-spin, language names, sign languages (all, none or only them), vitality levels and Typology (WALS).

In View › Typology (WALS) you choose one of 24 features – word order, adpositions, number of cases and genders, articles, tone, consonant inventory, negation, polar questions, numeral bases and more. The languages on the globe take the colour of their value and a key appears at the bottom right with the number of languages, a description of the feature and a link to the WALS chapter.

Click a value in the key to highlight only the languages with that value. Every language card has a Structure tab with all the features WALS describes for it; click a feature name to show it on the map. Only a sample of languages has data, the other dots stay grey.

On a language card click Compare with another language and pick the second one – on the globe, in the list or by searching. The atlas shows whether they are related and where they split, how their grammar differs and how many people speak them.
Tab moves between controls. One Tab takes you into the language list; move between tiles with the arrow keys, Home and End jump to the start and end. Enter selects a language.
The + and − keys zoom the globe. Escape closes a window, the card or a panel.

oddily.h: About, sources, contact, guide and calendar
p: At the very bottom of the language list (on a phone, at the end of the page) there is a folded line with a book: About, sources, contact, guide and calendar. Tap it to open it and tap again to fold it.

Calendar of language days: every day of the year when a language has its own celebration – a language day, a national holiday or an anniversary. It opens at the nearest day, and clicking a language shows it on the globe.
About the data: where the atlas gets its information about languages (Glottolog, WALS and more), how recent it is and why the list has a few more languages than there are dots on the globe.
Full guide: what you are reading right now.

Languages with a greeting (on the website only): every language with a greeting on one page. Each opens like a card in a card index; use the arrows to flip to the next one, and you can listen to the greeting.
Contact: send an idea or a mistake by email to info@atlasjazyku.cz. Below that are the data sources and their licences.
In the top right you can switch the page language (Česky) and the day or night look. The atlas remembers your choices.
The atlas also hides a few secrets. Try searching for elves or Klingons…
